Part 1

Who we are

TAIMATSU is not a software company. That turns out to be the most interesting thing about working here as an engineer.

1.1 The company

MUSASHI JAPAN

Japanese kitchen knives. It began in Kappabashi, Tokyo's kitchenware street, and now runs over 16 shops including a new one in Paris, with Hawaii next. The knives sell into more than 166 countries, and the checkout has to work from a kitchen in Ohio.

YOKAI JAPAN

It began as a sake bar, still running above the Kappabashi shop. Online it sells perfume and incense, which is now the front door of the brand.

FUJI JAPAN

Immersive experiences (blade sharpening, calligraphy) for visitors who want something other than a tour bus.

1.2 Why a knife company needs engineers

Selling to 166 countries means storefronts that work in several languages, load fast on a phone in a country you have never visited, and do not lose an order. That runs on Shopify. Selling to visitors inside Japan means tax-free processing, which is a regulated, paperwork-heavy process that most shops still do by hand at the till.

The first produced a team. The second produced a product: we run more than ten tax-free shops of our own, so the process was one we already knew from behind the counter, and it was worth building for properly.

Part 2

What we build

2.1 Online DX: the storefronts

Shopify already solved the cart, the payment and the inventory. What it does not solve is looking like the brand, in the right language, converting on a phone. That part is ours.

How we build it is changing. The shops running today are Liquid themes, Shopify’s own templating language. New work goes into Hydrogen, Shopify’s React framework: we keep Shopify’s checkout and inventory and talk to them over the Storefront API, but the storefront itself becomes ours to build, and to run. The team was already writing server code for custom Shopify apps and for automation used elsewhere in the company; Hydrogen adds the storefront to that list.

2.2 SAMURAI TAX: the refund platform

If you have bought something in Japan and shown your passport to skip the consumption tax, you have been on the customer side of this.

Japan lets tourists buy without paying the consumption tax. For the shop, that means checking a passport, recording the sale against the customer's entry record, and filing it correctly. Done by hand, at a till, with a queue behind the customer, in a language the clerk may not speak. It is slow and it is easy to get wrong.

samurai-tax.com

SAMURAI TAX is that process as software: a web app and a mobile app. The web app runs in any browser already in the shop, signed in as the shop, with no dedicated terminal. A camera makes it fast; typing the passport in by hand still works.

No setup fee, no monthly fee. We are paid out of the remittance fee the traveller pays when the tax is refunded, so we earn per refund rather than per subscription. That matters to how the thing is built: every completed refund is revenue, which is why the money path is the part that has to reconcile.

    Those four are only the half that happens at the till. The tourist then finishes onboarding on their own phone from the emailed link, and the money moves later, in a separate settlement run against the same database. A refund is a long-lived thing with several actors, not a form submission.

    Key point

    From November 2026 Japan switches tax-free retail to a refund model (リファンド方式): the customer pays the tax at the till, and is refunded once customs confirms the goods have actually left Japan. Every tax-free retailer in the country has to change how they operate.

    We are already running it, customs half included. A refund only completes after departure is confirmed, the traveller is told so at the point of sale, and the window on it is ninety days.

    That is the part that is genuinely hard to build, and it is why the problem here is not building a form. It is tracking someone else's money correctly for three months, across a border, and paying it out only once the goods are confirmed gone.

    Part 3

    The stack

    3.1 How the work is divided

    Who we work with

    Design and data do not sit inside engineering here. Worth knowing before you join rather than after.

    3.2 Layer by layer

    Key point

    Online DX does not rebuild what Shopify already provides: checkout, payment and inventory come from the platform. What the team writes is the storefront, custom Shopify apps, and automation for other departments across the company. SAMURAI TAX writes everything, because nobody had built it. Neither is a technology preference; both fall out of what the product is.

    What is interesting is that the two are now converging from opposite ends: Hydrogen brings React and TypeScript to the storefront side, so an engineer can move between our two products in a way that was not true a year ago.

    Part 4

    How we work, and where we are on hiring

    4.1 What the team is like

    🌏

    You do not need N1

    The company is close to an even split between Japanese and non-Japanese staff. N3 or N2 is usually enough to work here comfortably.

    🧩

    You will touch more than one layer

    A team this size does not have a person per layer. Most engineers here work across at least two.

    📐

    Correctness matters unevenly

    A storefront bug costs a sale. A refund bug costs someone's money and a filing. Knowing which one you are working on is part of the job.

    4.2 What we look for when we open a role

    Something you built end to end and can walk someone through, including the parts that went wrong. Evidence you can read a codebase you did not write. And the habit of asking what happens when the input is wrong, because on one of our two products that question is the whole job.

    What we usually open, when we open something, is frontend and backend roles where some mobile experience is a real advantage. So React, TypeScript and eventually React Native are the sensible things to put your next few months into. That would be our advice whether or not we were the ones hiring.

    Where we actually are

    We have no open positions today, but we hire steadily through the year.
